---
title: "Validation Against Known Communities"
subtitle: "Classifying 16S rRNA with DeepTaxa, and checking the result against a known composition"
---

The pages in this section apply the DeepTaxa workflow [@salah2026deeptaxa] to communities whose
composition is known in advance. Because the correct answer is available, these
examples measure accuracy directly rather than infer it, and they are the
recommended way to gain confidence in the tool before applying it to study samples.
Two regions are covered: the V3-V4 amplicon, which is the region most frequently
sequenced on Illumina platforms, and the full-length 16S gene, which supports
finer, species-level assignment.

## What the examples demonstrate

Each example follows the same path: install DeepTaxa, download the checkpoint that
matches the sequenced region, classify a set of amplicon sequence variants (ASVs),
interpret the confidence scores, and validate the result against the known
composition. The two pages differ in the region and in the depth of resolution they
reach.

- [V3-V4 mock community](validation/v3-v4.ipynb) classifies ASVs from the
  ZymoBIOMICS standard sequenced over V3-V4, and recovers all eight expected genera.
- [Full-length mock community](validation/full-length.ipynb) classifies full-length
  16S ASVs from the same standard, and examines species-level assignment, where
  DeepTaxa differs most from exact-matching reference classifiers.

Each notebook fetches its own inputs at runtime: the sequences and the reference tables
come from the data folder in the repository, and the checkpoint is downloaded from
Hugging Face. An "Open in Colab" badge at the top of each page lets the reader run the
notebook on a free GPU.

## Results and how to read them

At the genus rank, both DeepTaxa and the reference method recovered all eight expected
genera and agreed on the genus of essentially every read, so they are indistinguishable
there. The reference method here is DADA2 [@callahan2016dada2] with the SILVA v138
database [@quast2013silva], written DADA2 +
SILVA below: SILVA is the reference database, and DADA2 is the classifier, which uses a
naive Bayes model for the genus and exact matching for the species.

The methods differ at the species rank, and the difference is not the same in the two
regions. DADA2 + SILVA assigns a species only on an exact, unambiguous match: every
species it assigns is correct, so its precision is perfect, but it resolves few reads to
the species level and otherwise stays at the genus, declining to name a species rather
than naming one incorrectly. On the short V3-V4 region this caution is severe, and
DeepTaxa resolves far more reads to an exact species than the reference does. On the
full-length gene the two are close on exact matches, and DeepTaxa's advantage there is
coverage, not exactness.

That coverage is mostly close relatives that 16S cannot separate, such as the *Bacillus
subtilis* group or *Shigella* for *Escherichia coli*, which the figure credits in red.
One result is worth stating directly: none of DeepTaxa's species calls here is an
unrelated error; every miss is a near neighbor of the correct species within the same
genus. A few near neighbors are not credited, however: on some ASVs the reference
resolves the true species, for example *Salmonella enterica*, which DeepTaxa labels
*S. bongori*, and these are counted as misses, so the figure does not reward DeepTaxa
where the reference outperforms it. The net trade-off is that DeepTaxa commits to a
species far more often than the reference, at the cost of being occasionally wrong by
one near neighbor, while the reference abstains rather than committing.

![Reads correctly identified to species on the two mock communities. The genus rank is
omitted because both methods assign the correct genus to essentially every read. DADA2 +
SILVA assigns a species only by exact matching and abstains otherwise, so its lower
values reflect caution, not error; DeepTaxa also credits close relatives that 16S cannot
distinguish, in red. Near neighbors the reference does resolve, such as *Salmonella
enterica* labeled *S. bongori*, are counted as misses.](validation/overview-species.png)

## Three practical points

Three choices mostly decide whether a run is trustworthy, and the examples are built
around them.

The first, and the most important, is to match the checkpoint to the sequenced region.
The paper [@salah2026deeptaxa] puts a figure on the cost of getting this wrong: applying
the full-length checkpoint to V3-V4 reads lowers species accuracy from 92.96 percent to
60.7 percent, while a checkpoint trained on the V3-V4 window recovers most of the loss.
Classify V3-V4 reads with the V3-V4 checkpoint, and full-length reads with the
full-length checkpoint.

The second is to read the confidence score as a measure of how much information the
input carries, not as a promise that the call is correct. The score is well calibrated
on the held-out data, and it falls at the finer ranks, and on short or off-region reads,
because the marker carries less information there. A low score is the model declining to
commit, and filtering it out, for example below 0.5, is reasonable.

The third is easy to overlook: reconcile the taxonomy before scoring anything. DeepTaxa
reports the GTDB names used by Greengenes2 [@mcdonald2024greengenes], which renames or
splits several genera relative to the NCBI names on most reference materials.
*Lactobacillus fermentum*, for instance, becomes *Limosilactobacillus*. Without this
step, correct calls are counted as errors, and both notebooks include a short function
that handles it.
